title: Progression ladder: fin proportion and coding-site state across the beloniform series
read_this_first: A LADDER TO READ, NOT A TEST. Four groups (needlefish/saury, halfbeak, gliding halfbeak, flying fish) is far too few for any statistical claim. No correlation between residue state and fin ratio is computed: species share ancestry, so a cross-species correlation needs phylogenetic correction, and with four groups that correction cannot be done meaningfully.

THE NON-GLIDERS SCORE ZERO BY CONSTRUCTION. Sheet G lists only substitutions shared by gliders and ABSENT from outgroups, so non-gliding species carry the ancestral residue at these sites by definition; the zero is circular and is not a finding. The informative part of the ladder is among gliders: gliding halfbeaks (fin/SL about 0.27) carry about as many of these derived states as flying fishes (about 0.69), so derived-state count does not scale with fin length.

TRACKING IS NOT CAUSING. A residue that changes along with fin length across the series is consistent with involvement and is not evidence of causation. Our own causal chains grade slc43a2a (lat4a) at "mechanism".

A SLICE, NOT THE SYSTEM. Development means many genes are involved. The project gene map holds 4571 genes (genotype/pathways.slim.json, coverage.all_genes_in_vetted_map), 982 of them with expression records on the pectoral fin alone (genotype/README.md), and most between-species difference is regulatory rather than coding. Daane 2021 captured 105275 conserved non-coding elements (Zenodo medaka_cne_great.txt) alongside the coding exons, and reports accelerated non-coding evolution enriched in 455 GO terms on the flying-fish branch (sheet K) and 582 on the halfbeak branch (sheet M), against 44 convergent coding substitution rows (sheet G). The number of accelerated elements itself is NOT in Data S1 (the "# CNEs" column is a per-term total: the 118 terms shared by sheets K and M carry identical counts), so no like-for-like count of non-coding versus coding changes can be given from the local data. This short coding ladder is labelled as a slice through a much larger system, never as "the genes for wings".

sources.daane2021: Daane et al. 2021 Curr Biol, doi 10.1016/j.cub.2021.08.054, Data S1 (local genotype/cache/daane2021_data_s1_mmc2.xlsx, not redistributed)
sources.exons: Daane 2021 Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.5082978 (record 5082979) translated_exons.tar.gz, residues re-read here by blastp of the Ensembl 116 query protein against each species' captured exons (MIN identity 75%, best hit per region)

coordinate_system: Each site is numbered as in Daane 2021 sheet G: 1-based on the medaka protein (or, for rows whose Ensembl ID is from platyfish or Amazon molly, on that species' protein). The reference residue was checked against the Ensembl release 116 protein for that gene ID; rows where it no longer matches are listed under skipped_columns.
phylogeny_note: In the Zenodo species tree the two gliding-halfbeak genera are not sister to each other: Euleptorhamphus groups with Rhynchorhamphus, and Oxyporhamphus with Hemiramphus, so gliding arose more than once inside the halfbeak grade leading to flying fishes. That is why a residue shared by both gliding halfbeaks and flying fishes is called convergent.

non_coding_signal_per_branch.why_no_element_count: Data S1 does not report how many CNEs are accelerated on each branch. Its "# CNEs" column is the total number of captured CNEs assigned to the genes of each GO term: the 118 terms shared by sheets K and M have identical counts in both. Computing the accelerated count would need the Zenodo CNE alignments (cne.tar.gz, 153 MB) and a phyloP rerun, which was not done.
